cards.b: The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries.
The ridge of high land that separates one drainage basin from the next.
The point where a tributary joins a larger river.
Transpiration is water lost from plants through their leaves. Evaporation is liquid water turning to vapour from surfaces such as oceans and rivers.
Infiltration: water soaking into soil. Throughflow: moving sideways through soil. Percolation: moving down into rock.
Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution.
The force of water pushes air into cracks in the bank and bed, breaking off pieces of rock.
Abrasion: rocks carried by the river scrape the bed and banks. Attrition: rocks knock against each other and become smaller and rounder.
Solution (dissolved), suspension (fine particles in water), saltation (bounced), traction (rolled along the bed).
Discharge = cross-sectional area × velocity. Measured in cubic metres per second (cumecs).

cards.f: How do velocity and discharge change downstream?
cards.b: Both increase. Velocity rises because the channel is deeper and smoother (less friction); discharge rises as tributaries add water.
It gets smaller and more rounded because of attrition.
Formed in the upper course by vertical erosion, with weathering and mass movement wearing back the valley sides.
Ridges of hard land that overlap like zip teeth, because the river lacks the power to erode through them and winds around them.
Hard rock over soft rock. Soft rock eroded and undercut, plunge pool forms, overhang collapses, falls retreat upstream leaving a gorge.
Outside: fast flow, erosion, river cliff. Inside: slow flow, deposition, slip-off slope.
Meander neck narrows by erosion, river breaks through in a flood, deposition seals off the old loop.
The river floods, loses energy and drops its heaviest material next to the channel. Repeated floods build up raised banks.

short.q: Describe how the long profile of a river differs between its upper and lower courses.
short.model: The upper course is steep, while the lower course has a very gentle gradient. The long profile is concave, flattening towards the mouth.

short.q: Explain why velocity increases downstream even though the gradient decreases.
short.model: The channel becomes wider, deeper and smoother with smaller sediment, so there is less friction with the bed and banks. More water from tributaries also increases efficiency.
points: less friction with bed and banks

short.q: Explain how a flood plain forms.
short.model: When a river floods it slows and loses energy, so it deposits silt across the valley floor. Meanders also move sideways and deposit sediment, building a wide, flat flood plain.
points: river floods and loses energy, deposits silt
meanders migrate sideways / repeated flooding builds flat land

short.q: Give two factors that affect the rate of river erosion.
short.model: Geology (soft rock erodes faster than hard rock) and discharge or slope (steeper slopes and higher discharge give more energy for erosion).

short.q: Explain why the sediment in the lower course is smaller than in the upper course.
short.model: Rocks are broken down by attrition as they are carried downstream, so they become smaller and more rounded. Larger rocks are also deposited earlier when energy drops.
points: smaller and more rounded; bigger load dropped earlier
